title: Giani Ditt Singh
hook: a scholar from a family counted low became a leading Sikh writer

segments.voice: Yesterday, sabha, and your line was speak clearly. Did you say your one plain sentence? Today, one of the clearest voices that Sabha had. Day nine hundred sixty-three.

In a Punjab village, a boy is born into a family the caste order counts low. People like him are expected to work with their hands, keep their eyes down, and leave books to others. This boy doesn't. He learns to read. He learns poetry and argument. He studies with one religious teacher after another, asking hard questions. And one day, in Lahore, he's editing a Sikh newspaper in Punjabi. He's called Giani, the learned one. Today: Giani Ditt Singh.
screen: `A FAMILY COUNTED LOW.` → `A BOY WHO LEARNS TO READ.` → `EDITING A SIKH NEWSPAPER.`

segments.voice: First, the title. Giani means a learned one. In Sikh life it's a title for a person learned in the Gurus' word and able to explain it. Nobody is born a Giani. It's earned with years of study. Second, the search. Before he took the Khalsa's amrit, Ditt Singh moved through more than one religious circle, listening, reading, testing. When he came to the Gurus' path, he came as a thinker who had looked around, not as someone who'd never been asked. Third, the work. In Lahore he joined the Singh Sabha you met yesterday and became one of its sharpest writers. He edited the Khalsa Akhbar, a Punjabi paper of the reform, and wrote books and pamphlets in plain Punjabi: stories, verse, and arguments about what the Gurus taught. Tradition remembers him in public debate too. Fourth, why his birth matters to the story. Guru Nanak says, in a hymn in Asa, to recognize the divine light in each person and not to ask about their caste, because caste counts for nothing hereafter. The Lahore reformers said all Sikhs are equal before the Guru. Ditt Singh's own life put that teaching in plain view. Men of honored lineage sometimes sneered at his birth, and he answered them with his pen. In the Sikh tradition, his story says, learning isn't a family inheritance. It's open to anyone who sits down and does the work.
screen: `GIANI — A LEARNED ONE.` · `A SEEKER WHO LOOKED AROUND.` · `EDITOR AND WRITER IN LAHORE.` · `DON'T ASK ABOUT CASTE.` · then, large: `LEARNING FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Two minutes to honor a self-made scholar. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind someone who taught themselves, or who learned against the odds: a grandparent who read late at night, a coworker who studied after shifts, a writer whose story you know. Picture them at the table with the book open. Breathe in, and name one thing they learned. Breathe out, and wish them well, wherever they are. If you pray, you can hold them before Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Ditt Singh, born into a family counted low, who earned the title Giani, a learned one, and became a leading writer and editor of the Sikh reform. Today's word.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Giani Ditt Singh as a writer and editor of the Singh Sabha reform who rose from a family counted low, and the title Giani is still given to those learned in the Gurus' word.
